b3f8155c60: For a woman at the same height: 45.5 plus (2.3 times 10.9) equals about 70.5 kg, about 155 lb — illustrating the roughly 10 lb (4.5 kg) difference the formula applies between sexes at the same height.

ebb813f9e6: No single formula is best for everyone. Boer is widely used and generally reasonable for typical builds; if you have a measured body fat percentage (for example from DEXA), calculating lean mass directly from it is more accurate than any height-and-weight formula.

cf12c83617: Lean body mass (LBM) includes muscle, bone, organs and water — everything that isn't fat tissue. Each formula estimates it from weight (W, kg) and height (H, cm):
02d30a56b5: From body fat %: LBM = W × (1 − body fat ÷ 100) — the most direct option if you have a measured body fat figure.

69346c0d3a: Lean body mass is a useful figure for setting protein intake targets and for tracking body composition changes during training. Two people with the same total weight can have very different lean body mass, which is part of why weight alone is a limited measure of fitness or health. Clinically, lean mass is also used for dosing some medications.
dd3ef80d2f: A man weighing 80 kg at 180 cm. Boer: 0.407 × 80 + 0.267 × 180 − 19.2 = 32.6 + 48.1 − 19.2 = 61.4 kg lean mass, leaving 18.6 kg fat mass (about 23% body fat). James gives 62.7 kg and Hume 57.8 kg for the same inputs.
1015f63188: His FFMI is 61.4 ÷ 1.8² = 19.0; at exactly 1.8 m, the height-normalized FFMI is the same.
16d52bfe4d: Formula estimates become less precise at the extremes — very high muscle mass or very high body fat. The James formula in particular starts to fall as weight rises at high BMI, so it is unreliable above a BMI of about 35. Kouri et al. reported that FFMI values above about 25 were rare among drug-free male athletes, but FFMI calculated from a formula-based LBM carries the formula's error. DEXA scans and hydrostatic weighing measure body composition directly and are more accurate for people outside typical ranges.
